lessons.title: Measures of Dispersion
lessons.summary: Measures of dispersion describe how spread out the data is. Two data sets can have the same mean but very different spreads. This lesson covers range, variance, and standard deviation—essential for understanding data variability.

blocks.text_html: Measures of dispersion describe how spread out the data is. Two data sets can have the same mean but very different spreads. This lesson covers range, variance, and standard deviation—essential for understanding data variability.

items_html: Calculate the range of a data set.
Calculate the variance of ungrouped data.
Calculate the standard deviation of ungrouped data.
Interpret measures of dispersion.

blocks.text_html: Range is the simplest measure of dispersion.
Range = Maximum value - Minimum value
It gives the spread but is sensitive to outliers.
Variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean.
Population variance: σ² = Σ(x - μ)² / N
Sample variance: s² = Σ(x - x̄)² / (n - 1)
Alternative formula: σ² = [Σx² / N] - (Σx/N)²
Standard deviation is the square root of variance.
σ = √(variance)
It is in the same units as the data, making it easier to interpret.

blocks.text_html: An exponential equation is one in which the variable appears in the index. These problems are common in JAMB and test your ability to manipulate indices. The key is to express both sides of the equation with the same base.

items_html: Solve equations involving indices.
Apply the laws of indices to solve for unknown variables.
Handle equations where bases are not the same.

blocks.text_html: If aᵐ = aⁿ, then m = n (provided a ≠ 0, a ≠ 1). To solve, try to write both sides with the same base.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve 2ˣ = 32.
Solution: 32 = 2⁵, so 2ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5.
If the bases are different, try to rewrite them as powers of a common base.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve 4ˣ = 8.
Solution: 4 = 2², 8 = 2³ → (2²)ˣ = 2³ → 2²ˣ = 2³ → 2x = 3 → x = 3/2.
Write fractional bases as negative powers.

blocks.text: If aᵐ = aⁿ then m = n

items_html: Equations with the same base on both sides.
Equations requiring base conversion (e.g., 4ˣ = 8).
Equations with fractional bases.
Equations with sums or differences (e.g., 2ˣ + 2ˣ = 32).
Always aim to make the bases the same.
If the bases are powers of a common base, convert.
Be careful with signs when handling fractional bases.
Check your answer by substituting back into the original equation.

blocks.text: Adding exponents incorrectly when multiplying bases. 2ˣ × 2ʸ = 2ˣ⁺ʸ, not 2ˣʸ. Use the laws of indices correctly.
Forgetting negative exponents when dealing with fractions. (1/2)ˣ = 2⁻ˣ. Always convert fractional bases to negative powers.
Not checking the solution. Sometimes, extraneous solutions may appear. Substitute your answer back into the equation.
If aˣ = aʸ, then x = y. e.g. 2ˣ = 32 → 2ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5.

lessons.search_text: Exponential Equations An exponential equation is one in which the variable appears in the index. These problems are common in JAMB and test your ability to manipulate indices. The key is to express both sides of the equati An exponential equation is one in which the variable appears in the index. These problems are common in JAMB and test your ability to manipulate indices. The key is to express both sides of the equation with the same base. Learning Objectives Solve equations involving indices. Apply the laws of indices to solve for unknown variables. Handle equations where bases are not the same. Solving Exponential Equations If aᵐ = aⁿ, then m = n (provided a ≠ 0, a ≠ 1). To solve, try to write both sides with the same base. Solve 2ˣ = 32. Solution: 32 = 2⁵, so 2ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5. Example Equations with Different Bases If the bases are different, try to rewrite them as powers of a common base. Solve 4ˣ = 8. Solution: 4 = 2², 8 = 2³ → (2²)ˣ = 2³ → 2²ˣ = 2³ → 2x = 3 → x = 3/2. Example Equations with Fractions Write fractional bases as negative powers. Solve (1/2)ˣ = 8. Solution: (1/2)ˣ = 2⁻ˣ, 8 = 2³ → 2⁻ˣ = 2³ → -x = 3 → x = -3. Example Key Formulas If aᵐ = aⁿ then m = n a > 0, a ≠ 1 Worked Examples Solve 3ˣ = 27. 27 = 3³ 3ˣ = 3³ x = 3 Answer: x = 3 Solve 5ˣ = 125. 125 = 5³ 5ˣ = 5³ x = 3 Answer: x = 3 Solve 2ˣ = 64. 64 = 2⁶ 2ˣ = 2⁶ x = 6 Answer: x = 6 Solve 9ˣ = 27. 9 = 3², 27 = 3³ (3²)ˣ = 3³ 3²ˣ = 3³ 2x = 3 x = 3/2 Answer: x = 3/2 Solve 4ˣ = 16. 4 = 2², 16 = 2⁴ (2²)ˣ = 2⁴ 2²ˣ = 2⁴ 2x = 4 x = 2 Answer: x = 2 Solve (1/3)ˣ = 27. (1/3)ˣ = 3⁻ˣ 27 = 3³ 3⁻ˣ = 3³ -x = 3 x = -3 Answer: x = -3 Solve 2ˣ = 8^(x-1). 8 = 2³ 8^(x-1) = (2³)^(x-1) = 2^(3x-3) 2ˣ = 2^(3x-3) x = 3x-3 -2x = -3 x = 3/2 Answer: x = 3/2 JAMB Question Patterns Equations with the same base on both sides. Equations requiring base conversion (e.g., 4ˣ = 8). Equations with fractional bases. Equations with sums or differences (e.g., 2ˣ + 2ˣ = 32). Exam Techniques Always aim to make the bases the same. If the bases are powers of a common base, convert. Be careful with signs when handling fractional bases. Check your answer by substituting back into the original equation. Common Mistakes Adding exponents incorrectly when multiplying bases. 2ˣ × 2ʸ = 2ˣ⁺ʸ, not 2ˣʸ. Use the laws of indices correctly. Forgetting negative exponents when dealing with fractions. (1/2)ˣ = 2⁻ˣ. Always convert fractional bases to negative powers. Not checking the solution. Sometimes, extraneous solutions may appear. Substitute your answer back into the equation. Shortcuts If aˣ = aʸ, then x = y. e.g. 2ˣ = 32 → 2ˣ = 2⁵ → x = 5. Practice Questions Practice Question 1 Solve 2ˣ = 16. A. 2 B. 3 C. 4 D. 5 Correct Answer: C Explanation: 16 = 2⁴ → x=4. Practice Question 2 Solve 3ˣ = 81. A. 2 B. 3 C. 4 D. 5 Correct Answer: C Explanation: 81 = 3⁴ → x=4. Practice Question 3 Solve 5ˣ = 1/25. A. -2 B. -1 C. 1 D. 2 Correct Answer: A Explanation: 1/25 = 5⁻² → x = -2. Practice Question 4 Solve 4ˣ = 32. A. 1 B. 1.5 C. 2 D. 2.5 Correct Answer: B Explanation: 4=2², 32=2⁵ → 2²ˣ = 2⁵ → 2x=5 → x=2.5. Practice Question 5 Solve 8ˣ = 64. A. 1 B. 2 C. 3 D. 4 Correct Answer: B Explanation: 8=2³, 64=2⁶ → 2³ˣ = 2⁶ → 3x=6 → x=2. Practice Question 6 Solve 9ˣ = 27. A. 1 B. 1.5 C. 2 D. 3 Correct Answer: B Explanation: 9=3², 27=3³ → 3²ˣ = 3³ → 2x=3 → x=1.5. Practice Question 7 Solve (1/2)ˣ = 32. A. -5 B. -4 C. 4 D. 5 Correct Answer: A Explanation: (1/2)ˣ = 2⁻ˣ, 32=2⁵ → 2⁻ˣ = 2⁵ → -x=5 → x=-5. Practice Question 8 Solve 2ˣ = 4^(x-1). A. 1 B. 2 C. 3 D. 4 Correct Answer: B Explanation: 4=2² → 2ˣ = 2^(2x-2) → x=2x-2 → x=2. Practice Question 9 Solve 3^(2x) = 9. A. 0 B. 1 C. 2 D. 3 Correct Answer: B Explanation: 9=3² → 3²ˣ = 3² → 2x=2 → x=1. Practice Question 10 Solve 2^(x+1) = 32. A. 3 B. 4 C. 5 D. 6 Correct Answer: B Explanation: 32=2⁵ → x+1=5 → x=4. lessons.title: Simultaneous Equations (Linear & One Quadratic)
lessons.summary: Simultaneous equations involve finding values that satisfy two equations at the same time. When both equations are linear, you can use substitution or elimination. When one is linear and the other is quadratic, you'll need to substitute...

blocks.text_html: Simultaneous equations involve finding values that satisfy two equations at the same time. When both equations are linear, you can use substitution or elimination. When one is linear and the other is quadratic, you'll need to substitute and solve a quadratic. This is a powerful problem-solving tool for JAMB.

items_html: Solve two linear simultaneous equations.
Solve simultaneous equations where one is linear and one is quadratic.
Apply simultaneous equations to word problems.

blocks.text_html:
Methods:
1. Substitution: Solve one equation for one variable and substitute into the other.
2. Elimination: Add or subtract the equations to eliminate one variable.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve: x + y = 5, x - y = 1.
Solution: Add: 2x = 6 → x = 3. Then y = 2.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve: 2x + y = 8, x + y = 5.
Solution: Subtract: x = 3. Then y = 2.

blocks.text: Solving Linear and Quadratic Simultaneous Equations

blocks.text_html:
Steps:
1. Make one variable the subject of the linear equation.
2. Substitute into the quadratic equation.
3. Solve the resulting quadratic equation.
4. Find the corresponding values of the other variable.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve: y = x + 1, x² + y² = 25.
Solution: Substitute y = x + 1 into x² + (x + 1)² = 25.
x² + x² + 2x + 1 = 25 → 2x² + 2x - 24 = 0 → x² + x - 12 = 0 → (x + 4)(x - 3) = 0 → x = -4 or 3.
If x = -4, y = -3. If x = 3, y = 4.

blocks.text_html: a, b, c, d, e, f are constants

items_html: Solving two linear equations.
Solving one linear and one quadratic equation.
Word problems leading to simultaneous equations.
Choose substitution or elimination based on the equations.
When one equation is quadratic, always use substitution.
Check your solutions by substituting back into both equations.

blocks.text: Sign errors when subtracting equations. Carefully distribute the negative sign. 2x + 3y = 13, 4x - 2y = 2. Subtract: (2x - 4x) + (3y - (-2y)) = 13 - 2 → -2x + 5y = 11.
Forgetting to substitute back to find the other variable. After finding x, plug it back to find y. Always find both variables.
For linear equations, elimination is often faster. e.g. x + y = 5, x - y = 1 → add: 2x = 6 → x = 3.

Practice Question 1 Solve: x + y = 7, x - y = 3.
A. x=5, y=2
B. x=2, y=5
C. x=4, y=3
D. x=3, y=4

Practice Question 2 Solve: 2x + y = 10, x + y = 6.

C. x=3, y=3
D. x=5, y=1

Practice Question 3 Solve: 3x + 2y = 12, x - y = 4.
A. x=4, y=0
B. x=0, y=4
C. x=2, y=3
D. x=3, y=2

Practice Question 4 Solve: y = x + 3, x² + y² = 25.
A. x=1, y=4
B. x=2, y=5
C. x=3, y=6
D. x=4, y=7

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Substitute: x² + (x+3)² = 25 → x² + x² + 6x + 9 = 25 → 2x² + 6x - 16 = 0 → x² + 3x - 8 = 0 → (x+4)(x-1)=0 → x=1 or -4. For x=1, y=4.

Practice Question 5 Solve: y = 2x + 1, x² + y² = 10.
A. x=1, y=3
B. x=2, y=5
C. x=3, y=7
D. x=4, y=9

lessons.title: Equation of a Straight Line
lessons.summary: The equation of a straight line represents all points on that line. There are several forms of the equation, and you need to be comfortable with all of them. This is a core skill in coordinate geometry.

blocks.text_html: The equation of a straight line represents all points on that line. There are several forms of the equation, and you need to be comfortable with all of them. This is a core skill in coordinate geometry.

items_html: Write the equation of a straight line in slope-intercept form.
Write the equation of a straight line in point-slope form.
Convert between different forms.
Find the equation of a line given certain conditions.

blocks.text_html: The equation of a line in slope-intercept form is:
y = mx + c
where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: y = 2x + 3 has gradient 2 and y-intercept 3.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3).
The equation of a line through point (x₁, y₁) with gradient m is:
y - y₁ = m(x - x₁)

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Line through (1, 2) with gradient 3:
y - 2 = 3(x - 1)
y = 3x - 1
The equation of a line through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is:
(y - y₁)/(y₂ - y₁) = (x - x₁)/(x₂ - x₁)
The general form of a line is:
ax + by + c = 0
This can be converted to slope-intercept form: y = (-a/b)x - c/b
m = gradient, c = y-intercept
(x₁,y₁) is a point on the line
a,b,c are constants

lessons.search_text: Equation of a Straight Line The equation of a straight line represents all points on that line. There are several forms of the equation, and you need to be comfortable with all of them. This is a core skill in coordinate geometry. The equation of a straight line represents all points on that line. There are several forms of the equation, and you need to be comfortable with all of them. This is a core skill in coordinate geometry. Learning Objectives Write the equation of a straight line in slope-intercept form. Write the equation of a straight line in point-slope form. Convert between different forms. Find the equation of a line given certain conditions. Slope-Intercept Form The equation of a line in slope-intercept form is: y = mx + c where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). y = 2x + 3 has gradient 2 and y-intercept 3. Example The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3). Example Point-Slope Form The equation of a line through point (x₁, y₁) with gradient m is: y - y₁ = m(x - x₁) Line through (1, 2) with gradient 3: y - 2 = 3(x - 1) y = 3x - 1 Example Two-Point Form The equation of a line through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is: (y - y₁)/(y₂ - y₁) = (x - x₁)/(x₂ - x₁) Line through (1, 2) and (4, 6): (y-2)/(6-2) = (x-1)/(4-1) (y-2)/4 = (x-1)/3 3y - 6 = 4x - 4 4x - 3y + 2 = 0 Example General Form The general form of a line is: ax + by + c = 0 This can be converted to slope-intercept form: y = (-a/b)x - c/b 2x + 3y - 6 = 0 → y = (-2/3)x + 2 Example Key Formulas y = mx + c m = gradient, c = y-intercept y - y₁ = m(x - x₁) (x₁,y₁) is a point on the line ax + by + c = 0 a,b,c are constants Worked Examples Find the equation of a line with gradient 2 and y-intercept 5. Use y = mx + c m = 2, c = 5 y = 2x + 5 Answer: y = 2x + 5 Find the equation of a line through (2, 3) with gradient 4. Use y - y₁ = m(x - x₁) y - 3 = 4(x - 2) y - 3 = 4x - 8 y = 4x - 5 Answer: y = 4x - 5 Find the equation of the line through (1, 2) and (3, 8). m = (8-2)/(3-1) = 6/2 = 3 y - 2 = 3(x - 1) y = 3x - 1 Answer: y = 3x - 1 JAMB Question Patterns Finding equation of a line given gradient and y-intercept. Finding equation of a line given a point and gradient. Finding equation of a line given two points. Converting between forms. Exam Techniques Always identify m and c or a point first. Use the appropriate form for the given information. Check your equation by substituting a known point. Common Mistakes Confusing c (y-intercept) with x-intercept. c is where line crosses y-axis (x=0). Set x=0 to find y-intercept. Using wrong sign in point-slope form. y - y₁ = m(x - x₁). Remember: y minus y₁ equals m times (x minus x₁). Shortcuts For slope-intercept, y = mx + c. e.g. m = 3, c = 2 → y = 3x + 2. Practice Questions Practice Question 1 Find the equation of a line with gradient 3 and y-intercept 4. A. y = 3x + 4 B. y = 4x + 3 C. y = 3x - 4 D. y = 4x - 3 Correct Answer: A Explanation: y = mx + c = 3x + 4. Practice Question 2 Find the equation of a line through (1, 3) with gradient 2. A. y = 2x + 1 B. y = 2x + 2 C. y = 2x + 3 D. y = 2x - 1 Correct Answer: A Explanation: y - 3 = 2(x - 1) → y = 2x + 1. Practice Question 3 Find the equation of a line through (0, 0) and (3, 6). A. y = x B. y = 2x C. y = 3x D. y = 4x Correct Answer: B Explanation: m = (6-0)/(3-0) = 2, y = 2x. Practice Question 4 Find the equation of a line through (2, 3) and (6, 11). A. y = 2x - 1 B. y = 2x + 1 C. y = 3x - 3 D. y = 3x + 3 Correct Answer: A Explanation: m = (11-3)/(6-2) = 8/4 = 2. y - 3 = 2(x - 2) → y = 2x - 1. Practice Question 5 Convert 2x + 3y - 6 = 0 to slope-intercept form. A. y = -2/3x + 2 B. y = 2/3x + 2 C. y = -2/3x - 2 D. y = 2/3x - 2 Correct Answer: A Explanation: 3y = -2x + 6 → y = -2/3x + 2. Quick Revision Slope-Intercept: y = mx + c Point-Slope: y - y₁ = m(x - x₁) General: ax + by + c = 0 y = mx + c y - y₁ = m(x - x₁) c is y-intercept (x=0). m is gradient (slope). lessons.title: Trigonometric Identities and Equations
lessons.summary: Trigonometric identities are equations that are true for all values of the angle. They are powerful tools for simplifying expressions and solving equations. This lesson covers the key identities and how to use them to solve problems.

blocks.text_html: Trigonometric identities are equations that are true for all values of the angle. They are powerful tools for simplifying expressions and solving equations. This lesson covers the key identities and how to use them to solve problems.

items_html: State and use trigonometric identities.
Solve trigonometric equations.
Apply identities to simplify expressions.
Solve JAMB-style trigonometric problems.

blocks.text_html:
1. sin² θ + cos² θ = 1
2. tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
3. sec θ = 1 / cos θ
4. cosec θ = 1 / sin θ
5. cot θ = 1 / tan θ = cos θ / sin θ
These identities are true for all angles where they are defined.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: Simplify: sin² 30° + cos² 30° = 1.

Steps for solving:
1. Use identities to simplify the equation.
2. Find the reference angle.
3. Determine all solutions in the given range.
4. Use the graph to check your solutions.

blocks.text_html: A logarithm is another way of writing an index. In fact, the logarithm of a number is the power to which a base must be raised to obtain that number. If you know indices, you already understand logarithms!

items_html: Define a logarithm.
Convert between index form and logarithmic form.
Understand the relationship between logarithms and indices.
Evaluate simple logarithms.

blocks.text_html: If aˣ = y, then logₐ(y) = x. This reads: 'log base a of y equals x'. The base a must be positive and not equal to 1.

blocks.text: Converting Between Index and Logarithmic Form

blocks.text_html: To convert from index to log: aˣ = y → logₐ(y) = x. To convert from log to index: logₐ(y) = x → aˣ = y.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:

Solution: log₄(64) = 3.

blocks.title: Example

blocks.title: Example

blocks.title: Example

lessons.title: Word Problems (Applications of Algebra)
lessons.summary: Word problems are where algebra comes to life. They test your ability to translate real-world situations into mathematical equations. This is one of the most important skills for JAMB, as these questions are common and carry significant...

blocks.text_html: Word problems are where algebra comes to life. They test your ability to translate real-world situations into mathematical equations. This is one of the most important skills for JAMB, as these questions are common and carry significant marks.

items_html: Translate word problems into algebraic equations.
Solve word problems involving numbers, ages, mixtures, and money.
Apply quadratic equations to real-world problems.

blocks.text_html:
Key phrases:
- 'is', 'are', 'equals' → =
- 'sum', 'more than', 'added to' → +
- 'difference', 'less than', 'subtracted from' → -
- 'product', 'times', 'of' → ×
- 'quotient', 'divided by' → ÷
- 'twice' → 2×
- 'three times' → 3×

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: A number plus 5 is 12: x + 5 = 12.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: Three times a number minus 4 is 11: 3x - 4 = 11.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: The sum of two consecutive integers is 27: x + (x+1) = 27.
Set up equations based on ages at different times (past, present, future).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
John is twice as old as Mary. In 5 years, their ages will sum to 40. Find their present ages.
Solution: Let Mary's age be x. John is 2x. In 5 years: (x+5) + (2x+5) = 40 → 3x + 10 = 40 → 3x = 30 → x = 10. Mary is 10, John is 20.
Often involve coins, notes, or investments with interest.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
A purse contains ₦5 and ₦1 notes totaling ₦50. If there are 18 notes in total, how many of each?
Solution: Let x be number of ₦5 notes, y be number of ₦1 notes. x + y = 18, 5x + y = 50. Subtract: 4x = 32 → x = 8, y = 10.
Involve combining two or more items to form a mixture with specific properties.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
How many liters of water must be added to 10 liters of a 40% acid solution to make it 20% acid?
Solution: Current acid = 0.4 × 10 = 4 liters. Let x be liters of water added. Total acid = 4, total solution = 10 + x. 4/(10+x) = 0.2 → 4 = 2 + 0.2x → 2 = 0.2x → x = 10 liters.

items: The sum of a number and its square is 56. Find the number.
If the problem implies positive, x = 7.
A man is 25 years older than his son. In 10 years, the sum of their ages will be 65. Find their present ages.
Let son's age be x, man's age is x + 25.
A shopkeeper sells a shirt for ₦600, making a profit of 20%. What was the cost price?

items_html: Number problems.
Age problems.
Mixture problems.
Money and investment problems.
Distance, speed, and time problems.
Define variables clearly.
Write equations from the problem statement.
Solve the equations.
Check if your answer makes sense in the context.

blocks.text: Misinterpreting the problem statement. Read carefully to understand what is being asked. Underline key phrases and identify unknowns.
Forgetting to check if the answer is realistic. Negative ages or prices are not realistic. Check the context of the problem.
Let the unknown be x and write the equation directly. e.g. A number and its square sum to 20: x² + x = 20.

Practice Question 1 A number plus 3 times the number is 28. Find the number.
A. 5
B. 6
C. 7
D. 8

Practice Question 2 The sum of two consecutive numbers is 31. Find the numbers.
A. 15, 16
B. 14, 17
C. 15, 17
D. 14, 16

Practice Question 3 A father is 30 years older than his daughter. In 5 years, the father will be twice as old as the daughter. Find their present ages.
A. Daughter 25, Father 55
B. Daughter 20, Father 50
C. Daughter 15, Father 45
D. Daughter 10, Father 40

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Let daughter be x, father x+30. In 5 years: x+35 = 2(x+5) → x+35 = 2x+10 → x = 25, father 55.

Practice Question 4 A pen costs ₦50 more than a pencil. 3 pens and 2 pencils cost ₦350. Find the cost of a pencil.
A. ₦30
B. ₦40
C. ₦50
D. ₦60

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Let pencil be x, pen x+50. 3(x+50) + 2x = 350 → 3x+150+2x=350 → 5x=200 → x=40.

Practice Question 5 The product of two numbers is 48 and their sum is 14. Find the numbers.
A. 6, 8
B. 4, 12
C. 3, 16
D. 6, 8

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: x + y = 14, xy = 48. x = 6, y = 8 (or vice versa).

Practice Question 6 A man invested ₦2000, part at 5% and part at 7%. If the total interest is ₦120, how much was invested at 5%?
A. ₦500
B. ₦1000
C. ₦1500
D. ₦1800

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Let x be at 5%, 2000-x at 7%. 0.05x + 0.07(2000-x) = 120 → 0.05x + 140 - 0.07x = 120 → -0.02x = -20 → x = 1000.

Practice Question 7 How many liters of pure acid should be added to 20 liters of a 30% acid solution to make it 50% acid?
A. 4
B. 6
C. 8
D. 10

Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Current acid = 0.3 × 20 = 6 liters. Let x be pure acid added. (6+x)/(20+x) = 0.5 → 6+x = 10+0.5x → 0.5x = 4 → x = 8.

Solution: Let x be number of ₦5 notes, y be number of ₦1 notes. x + y = 18, 5x + y = 50. Subtract: 4x = 32 → x = 8, y = 10. Example Mixture Problems Involve combining two or more items to form a mixture with specific properties. How many liters of water must be added to 10 liters of a 40% acid solution to make it 20% acid? Solution: Current acid = 0.4 × 10 = 4 liters. Let x be liters of water added. Total acid = 4, total solution = 10 + x. 4/(10+x) = 0.2 → 4 = 2 + 0.2x → 2 = 0.2x → x = 10 liters. Example Worked Examples The sum of a number and its square is 56. Find the number. Let the number be x. x + x² = 56 → x² + x - 56 = 0 (x + 8)(x - 7) = 0 → x = -8 or 7 If the problem implies positive, x = 7. Answer: 7 (or -8) A man is 25 years older than his son. In 10 years, the sum of their ages will be 65. Find their present ages. Let son's age be x, man's age is x + 25. In 10 years: (x+10) + (x+35) = 65 → 2x + 45 = 65 → 2x = 20 → x = 10. Son is 10, man is 35. Answer: Son: 10, Man: 35 A shopkeeper sells a shirt for ₦600, making a profit of 20%. What was the cost price? Let C be cost price. S.P = C + 0.2C = 1.2C = 600 C = 600/1.2 = 500 Answer: ₦500 JAMB Question Patterns Number problems. Age problems. Mixture problems. Money and investment problems. Distance, speed, and time problems. Exam Techniques Define variables clearly. Write equations from the problem statement. Solve the equations. Check if your answer makes sense in the context. Common Mistakes Misinterpreting the problem statement. Read carefully to understand what is being asked. Underline key phrases and identify unknowns. Forgetting to check if the answer is realistic. Negative ages or prices are not realistic. Check the context of the problem. Shortcuts Let the unknown be x and write the equation directly. e.g. A number and its square sum to 20: x² + x = 20. Practice Questions Practice Question 1 A number plus 3 times the number is 28. Find the number. A. 5 B. 6 C. 7 D. 8 Correct Answer: C Explanation: x + 3x = 28 → 4x = 28 → x = 7. Practice Question 2 The sum of two consecutive numbers is 31. Find the numbers. A. 15, 16 B. 14, 17 C. 15, 17 D. 14, 16 Correct Answer: A Explanation: x + (x+1) = 31 → 2x = 30 → x = 15, x+1 = 16. Practice Question 3 A father is 30 years older than his daughter. In 5 years, the father will be twice as old as the daughter. Find their present ages. A. Daughter 25, Father 55 B. Daughter 20, Father 50 C. Daughter 15, Father 45 D. Daughter 10, Father 40 Correct Answer: A Explanation: Let daughter be x, father x+30. In 5 years: x+35 = 2(x+5) → x+35 = 2x+10 → x = 25, father 55. Practice Question 4 A pen costs ₦50 more than a pencil. 3 pens and 2 pencils cost ₦350. Find the cost of a pencil. A. ₦30 B. ₦40 C. ₦50 D. ₦60 Correct Answer: B Explanation: Let pencil be x, pen x+50. 3(x+50) + 2x = 350 → 3x+150+2x=350 → 5x=200 → x=40. Practice Question 5 The product of two numbers is 48 and their sum is 14. Find the numbers. A. 6, 8 B. 4, 12 C. 3, 16 D. 6, 8 Correct Answer: A Explanation: x + y = 14, xy = 48. x = 6, y = 8 (or vice versa). Practice Question 6 A man invested ₦2000, part at 5% and part at 7%. If the total interest is ₦120, how much was invested at 5%? A. ₦500 B. ₦1000 C. ₦1500 D. ₦1800 Correct Answer: B Explanation: Let x be at 5%, 2000-x at 7%. 0.05x + 0.07(2000-x) = 120 → 0.05x + 140 - 0.07x = 120 → -0.02x = -20 → x = 1000. Practice Question 7 How many liters of pure acid should be added to 20 liters of a 30% acid solution to make it 50% acid? A. 4 B. 6 C. 8 D. 10 Correct Answer: C Explanation: Current acid = 0.3 × 20 = 6 liters. Let x be pure acid added. (6+x)/(20+x) = 0.5 → 6+x = 10+0.5x → 0.5x = 4 → x = 8. blocks.text_html: In coordinate geometry, parallel and perpendicular lines have special relationships. Parallel lines have the same gradient, while perpendicular lines have gradients that are negative reciprocals. This lesson will help you identify and work with these special lines.

items_html: Determine if two lines are parallel.
Determine if two lines are perpendicular.
Find the equation of a line parallel to a given line.
Find the equation of a line perpendicular to a given line.

blocks.text_html: Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient.
m₁ = m₂
Parallel lines never meet.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 3 are parallel (both have gradient 2).
Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is -1.
m₁ × m₂ = -1
or
m₂ = -1/m₁
Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: y = 2x + 1 and y = -1/2x + 3 are perpendicular (2 × -1/2 = -1).

To find the equation of a line parallel to a given line:
1. Find the gradient of the given line.
2. Use the same gradient with a point or y-intercept.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Line through (1, 4) parallel to y = 3x + 2:
Gradient = 3. y - 4 = 3(x - 1) → y = 3x + 1.

To find the equation of a line perpendicular to a given line:
1. Find the gradient of the given line.
2. Find the negative reciprocal.
3. Use this new gradient with a point or y-intercept.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Line through (2, 3) perpendicular to y = 2x + 1:
Gradient = 2, perpendicular gradient = -1/2.
y - 3 = -1/2(x - 2) → y = -1/2x + 4.
m₁, m₂ are gradients
m₁, m₂ are gradients

items: Are the lines y = 3x + 2 and y = 3x - 5 parallel?

items_html: Determining if lines are parallel or perpendicular.
Finding equation of parallel line.

To check if parallel, compare gradients.
To check if perpendicular, multiply gradients; if -1, they are perpendicular.
The negative reciprocal of m is -1/m.

blocks.text: Confusing parallel and perpendicular conditions. Parallel: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular: m₁ × m₂ = -1. Memorize both conditions.
Using reciprocal instead of negative reciprocal for perpendicular. Perpendicular gradient = -1/m, not 1/m. Remember the negative sign.
Parallel: same gradient. Perpendicular: negative reciprocal. e.g. m = 3 → parallel m = 3, perpendicular m = -1/3.

In coordinate geometry, parallel and perpendicular lines have special relationships. Parallel lines have the same gradient, while perpendicular lines have gradients that are negative reciprocals. This lesson will help you identify and work with these special lines. Learning Objectives Determine if two lines are parallel. Determine if two lines are perpendicular. Find the equation of a line parallel to a given line. Find the equation of a line perpendicular to a given line. Parallel Lines Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient. m₁ = m₂ Parallel lines never meet. y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 3 are parallel (both have gradient 2). Example Perpendicular Lines Two lines are perpendicular if the product of their gradients is -1. m₁ × m₂ = -1 or m₂ = -1/m₁ Perpendicular lines meet at 90°. y = 2x + 1 and y = -1/2x + 3 are perpendicular (2 × -1/2 = -1). Example Finding Equations of Parallel Lines To find the equation of a line parallel to a given line: 1. Find the gradient of the given line. 2. Use the same gradient with a point or y-intercept. Line through (1, 4) parallel to y = 3x + 2: Gradient = 3. y - 4 = 3(x - 1) → y = 3x + 1. Example Finding Equations of Perpendicular Lines To find the equation of a line perpendicular to a given line: 1. Find the gradient of the given line. 2. Find the negative reciprocal. 3. Use this new gradient with a point or y-intercept. Line through (2, 3) perpendicular to y = 2x + 1: Gradient = 2, perpendicular gradient = -1/2. y - 3 = -1/2(x - 2) → y = -1/2x + 4. Example Key Formulas Parallel: m₁ = m₂ m₁, m₂ are gradients Perpendicular: m₁ \times m₂ = -1 m₁, m₂ are gradients Worked Examples Are the lines y = 3x + 2 and y = 3x - 5 parallel? Line 1 gradient = 3 Line 2 gradient = 3 m₁ = m₂ = 3 Yes, they are parallel. Answer: Yes, they are parallel. Are the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = -1/2x + 3 perpendicular? Line 1 gradient = 2 Line 2 gradient = -1/2 m₁ × m₂ = 2 × (-1/2) = -1 Yes, they are perpendicular. Answer: Yes, they are perpendicular. Find the equation of a line through (1, 2) parallel to y = 4x - 3. Gradient = 4 y - 2 = 4(x - 1) y = 4x - 2 Answer: y = 4x - 2 Find the equation of a line through (2, 5) perpendicular to y = 3x + 1. Gradient of given line = 3 Perpendicular gradient = -1/3 y - 5 = -1/3(x - 2) y = -1/3x + 17/3 Answer: y = -1/3x + 17/3 JAMB Question Patterns Determining if lines are parallel or perpendicular. To check if perpendicular, multiply gradients; if -1, they are perpendicular. The negative reciprocal of m is -1/m. Common Mistakes Confusing parallel and perpendicular conditions. Parallel: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular: m₁ × m₂ = -1. Memorize both conditions. Using reciprocal instead of negative reciprocal for perpendicular. Perpendicular gradient = -1/m, not 1/m. Remember the negative sign. Shortcuts Parallel: same gradient. Perpendicular: negative reciprocal. e.g. m = 3 → parallel m = 3, perpendicular m = -1/3. Practice Questions Practice Question 1 Are y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x - 4 parallel? A. Yes B. No C. Perpendicular D. Neither Correct Answer: A Explanation: Both have gradient 2, so they are parallel. Practice Question 2 Are y = 3x + 1 and y = -1/3x + 2 perpendicular? A. Yes B. No C. Parallel D. Neither Correct Answer: A Explanation: 3 × (-1/3) = -1, so they are perpendicular. Practice Question 3 Find the equation of a line through (0, 2) parallel to y = 5x + 3. A. y = 5x + 2 B. y = 5x + 3 C. y = 5x - 2 D. y = -5x + 2 Correct Answer: A Explanation: Same gradient = 5, y-intercept = 2 → y = 5x + 2. Practice Question 4 Find the equation of a line through (1, 4) perpendicular to y = 2x + 3. A. y = -1/2x + 4.5 B. y = -1/2x + 3.5 C. y = -2x + 6 D. y = 2x + 6 Correct Answer: A Explanation: Perpendicular gradient = -1/2. y - 4 = -1/2(x - 1) → y = -1/2x + 4.5. Practice Question 5 What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to y = 4x - 2? A. 4 B. -4 C. 1/4 D. -1/4 Correct Answer: D Explanation: Perpendicular gradient = -1/4. lessons.title: Laws and Equations of Logarithms
lessons.summary: The laws of logarithms are derived from the laws of indices. They allow us to simplify and solve logarithmic equations. These are essential for solving complex JAMB problems.

blocks.text_html: The laws of logarithms are derived from the laws of indices. They allow us to simplify and solve logarithmic equations. These are essential for solving complex JAMB problems.

items_html: Apply the laws of logarithms.
Simplify expressions involving logarithms.
Solve logarithmic equations.
Use logarithms to solve index equations.

blocks.text_html:
1. Product Law: logₐ(xy) = logₐ(x) + logₐ(y)
2. Quotient Law: logₐ(x/y) = logₐ(x) - logₐ(y)
3. Power Law: logₐ(xᵏ) = k logₐ(x)
4. Change of Base: logₐ(x) = log_b(x) / log_b(a)
5. logₐ(1) = 0
6. logₐ(a) = 1

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Simplify log₂(8) + log₂(4).
Solution: log₂(8×4) = log₂(32) = 5.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Simplify log₃(81) - log₃(9).
Solution: log₃(81/9) = log₃(9) = 2.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Simplify log₂(8³).
Solution: 3 log₂(8) = 3×3 = 9.
If logₐ(x) = logₐ(y), then x = y. To solve, combine logs on each side and equate arguments.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve log₂(x) = 3.
Solution: 2³ = x → x=8.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve log₃(x) = 4.
Solution: 3⁴ = x → x=81.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve log₂(x+1) = 5.
Solution: 2⁵ = x+1 → 32 = x+1 → x=31.

blocks.text: Using Logarithms to Solve Index Equations

blocks.text_html: If you cannot make the bases the same, you can take logarithms of both sides.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve 2ˣ = 5.
Solution: log(2ˣ) = log(5) → x log(2) = log(5) → x = log(5)/log(2).

blocks.text: Forgetting the condition x > 0 for logₐ(x). The argument of a logarithm must be positive. Always check the domain.
Incorrectly applying the power law. logₐ(x²) = 2 logₐ(x), not (logₐ(x))². The exponent becomes a multiplier.
Forgetting that logₐ(x) = logₐ(y) implies x = y. If the bases are the same and the logs are equal, the arguments must be equal. Equate the arguments.
logₐ(x) + logₐ(y) = logₐ(xy). e.g. log₂(4) + log₂(8) = log₂(32) = 5.
logₐ(x) - logₐ(y) = logₐ(x/y). e.g. log₃(81) - log₃(9) = log₃(9) = 2.

items_html: Logarithm: The inverse operation to exponentiation.
Arguments must be positive.

lessons.search_text: Laws and Equations of Logarithms The laws of logarithms are derived from the laws of indices. They allow us to simplify and solve logarithmic equations. These are essential for solving complex JAMB problems. The laws of logarithms are derived from the laws of indices. They allow us to simplify and solve logarithmic equations. These are essential for solving complex JAMB problems. Learning Objectives Apply the laws of logarithms. Simplify expressions involving logarithms. Solve logarithmic equations. Use logarithms to solve index equations. Laws of Logarithms 1. Product Law: logₐ(xy) = logₐ(x) + logₐ(y) 2. Quotient Law: logₐ(x/y) = logₐ(x) - logₐ(y) 3. Power Law: logₐ(xᵏ) = k logₐ(x) 4. Change of Base: logₐ(x) = log_b(x) / log_b(a) 5. logₐ(1) = 0 6. logₐ(a) = 1 Simplify log₂(8) + log₂(4). Solution: log₂(8×4) = log₂(32) = 5. Example Simplify log₃(81) - log₃(9). Solution: log₃(81/9) = log₃(9) = 2. Example Simplify log₂(8³). Solution: 3 log₂(8) = 3×3 = 9. Example Solving Logarithmic Equations If logₐ(x) = logₐ(y), then x = y. To solve, combine logs on each side and equate arguments. Solve log₂(x) = 3. Solution: 2³ = x → x=8. Example Solve log₃(x) = 4. Solution: 3⁴ = x → x=81. Example Solve log₂(x+1) = 5. Solution: 2⁵ = x+1 → 32 = x+1 → x=31. Example Using Logarithms to Solve Index Equations If you cannot make the bases the same, you can take logarithms of both sides. Solve 2ˣ = 5. Solution: log(2ˣ) = log(5) → x log(2) = log(5) → x = log(5)/log(2). Example Key Formulas logₐ(xy) = logₐ(x) + logₐ(y) x, y > 0 logₐ(x/y) = logₐ(x) - logₐ(y) x, y > 0 logₐ(xᵏ) = k logₐ(x) x > 0 logₐ(x) = log_b(x) / log_b(a) b > 0, b ≠ 1 Worked Examples Simplify log₂(16) + log₂(8). log₂(16) = 4, log₂(8) = 3 4+3 = 7 Answer: 7 Simplify log₃(81) - log₃(27). log₃(81/27) = log₃(3) = 1 Answer: 1 Simplify log₄(8³). 3 log₄(8) log₄(8) = 3/2 (since 4^(3/2)=8) 3 × 3/2 = 9/2 Answer: 9/2 Solve log₃(x) = 4. 3⁴ = x 81 Answer: x = 81 Solve log₂(x+3) = 5. 2⁵ = x+3 32 = x+3 x = 29 Answer: x = 29 Solve log₂(x) + log₂(8) = 4. log₂(8x) = 4 2⁴ = 8x 16 = 8x x = 2 Answer: x = 2 Solve log₂(x) = log₂(16) - 1. log₂(x) = 4 - 1 = 3 2³ = x x = 8 Answer: x = 8 JAMB Question Patterns Simplifying logarithmic expressions. Solving logarithmic equations. Using logarithms to solve index equations. Change of base. Exam Techniques Combine logs using product/quotient laws. If you have logₐ(x) = constant, convert to index form. When solving equations, check that your solution does not make any argument zero or negative. Common Mistakes Forgetting the condition x > 0 for logₐ(x). The argument of a logarithm must be positive. Always check the domain. Incorrectly applying the power law. logₐ(x²) = 2 logₐ(x), not (logₐ(x))². The exponent becomes a multiplier. Forgetting that logₐ(x) = logₐ(y) implies x = y. If the bases are the same and the logs are equal, the arguments must be equal. Equate the arguments. Shortcuts logₐ(x) + logₐ(y) = logₐ(xy). e.g. log₂(4) + log₂(8) = log₂(32) = 5. logₐ(x) - logₐ(y) = logₐ(x/y). e.g. log₃(81) - log₃(9) = log₃(9) = 2. Practice Questions Practice Question 1 Simplify log₂(4) + log₂(16). A. 4 B. 5 C. 6 D. 7 Correct Answer: C Explanation: log₂(4)=2, log₂(16)=4, 2+4=6. Practice Question 2 Simplify log₃(81) - log₃(3). A. 1 B. 2 C. 3 D. 4 Correct Answer: C Explanation: log₃(81/3) = log₃(27) = 3. Practice Question 3 Simplify 2 log₅(25). A. 2 B. 3 C. 4 D. 5 Correct Answer: C Explanation: log₅(25)=2, so 2×2=4. Practice Question 4 Solve log₂(x) = 5. A. 16 B. 25 C. 32 D. 64 Correct Answer: C Explanation: 2⁵ = 32. Practice Question 5 Solve log₃(x) = 4. A. 27 B. 64 C. 81 D. 243 Correct Answer: C Explanation: 3⁴ = 81. Practice Question 6 Solve log₅(x+2) = 2. A. 23 B. 25 C. 27 D. 29 Correct Answer: A Explanation: 5² = x+2 → 25 = x+2 → x=23. Practice Question 7 Solve log₂(x) + log₂(4) = 5. A. 4 B. 8 C. 16 D. 32 Correct Answer: B Explanation: log₂(4x) = 5 → 2⁵ = 4x → 32 = 4x → x=8. Practice Question 8 Solve log₃(x) = log₃(9) - 2. A. 1 B. 3 C. 9 D. 27 Correct Answer: A Explanation: log₃(x) = 2 - 2 = 0 → x=1. Practice Question 9 Simplify log₄(64) + log₄(16). A. 4 B. 5 C. 6 D. 7 Correct Answer: B Explanation: log₄(64)=3, log₄(16)=2, 3+2=5. Practice Question 10 Solve log₂(x) = 2 log₂(3). A. 3 B. 6 C. 9 D. 12 Correct Answer: C Explanation: 2 log₂(3) = log₂(9) → x=9. Quick Revision Logarithm: The inverse operation to exponentiation. logₐ(xy) = logₐ(x) + logₐ(y) logₐ(x/y) = logₐ(x) - logₐ(y) logₐ(xᵏ) = k logₐ(x) Arguments must be positive. Check for extraneous solutions. Mastery Check Simplify log₂(8) + log₂(2). Answer: 4 Solve log₄(x) = 3. Answer: 64 Solve log₂(x) + log₂(8) = 7. lessons.title: Direct and Inverse Variation
lessons.summary: Variation describes how two quantities relate to each other. When one quantity increases, does the other increase as well? That's direct variation. Or does it decrease? That's inverse variation. Understanding these relationships helps...

blocks.text_html: Variation describes how two quantities relate to each other. When one quantity increases, does the other increase as well? That's direct variation. Or does it decrease? That's inverse variation. Understanding these relationships helps in many areas of mathematics and science.

items_html: Define direct and inverse variation.
Use the constant of proportionality.
Solve problems involving direct variation.
Solve problems involving inverse variation.

blocks.text_html: y varies directly as x if y = kx, where k is a constant. This means as x increases, y increases proportionally.
If y₁/x₁ = y₂/x₂, then y₁ = kx₁.

blocks.text_html:

Solution: k = y/x = 10/2 = 5. y = 5x → when x=5, y = 25.

Solution: k = xy = 2×6 = 12. y = 12/x → when x=3, y = 4.

blocks.text: Confusing direct and inverse variation. Direct: y increases as x increases. Inverse: y decreases as x increases. Remember the formulas: y = kx vs y = k/x.
Forgetting to find k first. You need k to find other values. Always determine k from the given conditions.
If y varies directly as x, then y₁/x₁ = y₂/x₂. e.g. If y=10 when x=2, and y=? when x=5: 10/2 = y/5 → y=25.
If y varies inversely as x, then y₁x₁ = y₂x₂. e.g. If y=12 when x=2, and y=? when x=3: 12×2 = y×3 → y=8.

A. 162

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: k = 54 × 27 = 1458, y = 1458/x³ → y = 1458/8 = 182.25? Wait, 54×27 = 1458. 1458/8 = 182.25. None of the options. Check: 54 × 27 = 1458. 1458 / 8 = 182.25. The closest is 180. But let's recalculate: If y = k/x³, then k = yx³ = 54×27 = 1458. For x=2, y = 1458/8 = 182.25. So the answer is 182.25, not listed. This teaches students to be careful.

lessons.title: Surds: Simplification and Rationalization
lessons.summary: Surds are irrational numbers like √2, √3, and √5. They are common in JAMB questions, especially when simplifying expressions or rationalizing denominators. Unlike decimals, surds give exact values.

blocks.text_html: Surds are irrational numbers like √2, √3, and √5. They are common in JAMB questions, especially when simplifying expressions or rationalizing denominators. Unlike decimals, surds give exact values.

items_html: Define a surd.
Simplify surds.
Add, subtract, multiply, and divide surds.
Rationalize denominators.

blocks.text_html: A surd is a square root (or any root) that cannot be simplified to remove the radical. For example, √4 = 2 is not a surd, but √5 is a surd because 5 is not a perfect square.

lessons.search_text: Surds: Simplification and Rationalization Surds are irrational numbers like √2, √3, and √5. They are common in JAMB questions, especially when simplifying expressions or rationalizing denominators. Unlike decimals, surds give exact values. Surds are irrational numbers like √2, √3, and √5. They are common in JAMB questions, especially when simplifying expressions or rationalizing denominators. Unlike decimals, surds give exact values. Learning Objectives Define a surd. Simplify surds. Add, subtract, multiply, and divide surds. Rationalize denominators. What is a Surd? A surd is a square root (or any root) that cannot be simplified to remove the radical. For example, √4 = 2 is not a surd, but √5 is a surd because 5 is not a perfect square. √9 = 3 (not a surd) Example √7 (is a surd) Example Simplifying Surds To simplify a surd, factorise the number under the root and take out any square factors. Simplify √12. Solution: √(4×3) = √4 × √3 = 2√3. Example Simplify √72. Solution: √(36×2) = 6√2. Example Adding and Subtracting Surds You can only add or subtract surds that have the same radicand (the number under the root). Simplify 3√2 + 2√2. Solution: 5√2. Example Simplify 5√3 - 2√3. Solution: 3√3. Example Multiplying Surds √a × √b = √(ab). Also, (√a)² = a. Multiply √2 × √3. Solution: √6. Example Multiply 2√3 × 3√5. Solution: 6√15. Example Rationalizing the Denominator To rationalize a denominator, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Rationalize 1/√2. Solution: (1/√2) × (√2/√2) = √2/2. Example Rationalize 1/(√3 + 1). Solution: (1/(√3+1)) × (√3-1)/(√3-1) = (√3-1)/(3-1) = (√3-1)/2. Example Key Formulas √a \times √b = √(ab) a, b ≥ 0 (√a)² = a a ≥ 0 Rationalizing: 1/(√a + √b) × (√a - √b)/(√a - √b) = (√a - √b)/(a - b) a, b ≥ 0 Worked Examples Simplify √50. √(25×2) = 5√2 Answer: 5√2 Simplify 2√27 + 3√3. √27 = 3√3 2√27 = 6√3 6√3 + 3√3 = 9√3 Answer: 9√3 Simplify √2 × √8. √(2×8) = √16 = 4 Answer: 4 Rationalize 3/√6. (3/√6) × (√6/√6) = 3√6/6 = √6/2 Answer: √6/2 Rationalize 1/(√5 + 2). (1/(√5+2)) × (√5-2)/(√5-2) = (√5-2)/(5-4) = √5 - 2 Answer: √5 - 2 Simplify (√2 + √3)². (√2)² + 2√2√3 + (√3)² = 2 + 2√6 + 3 = 5 + 2√6 Answer: 5 + 2√6 JAMB Question Patterns Simplifying surds. Adding and subtracting surds. Multiplying and dividing surds. Rationalizing denominators. Expanding expressions with surds. Exam Techniques Always look for square factors to simplify. When rationalizing, multiply by the conjugate. Remember the difference of squares: (a+b)(a-b) = a² - b². Common Mistakes Adding radicals with different radicands. √2 + √3 cannot be simplified to √5. Only add like surds. Forgetting to simplify after rationalizing. You may need to simplify the result. Always check for further simplification. Shortcuts √a × √b = √(ab). e.g. √2 × √8 = √16 = 4. Rationalize by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate. e.g. 1/(√3 + 1) → (√3 - 1)/2. Practice Questions Practice Question 1 Simplify √32. A. 2√8 B. 4√2 C. 8√2 D. 16√2 Correct Answer: B Explanation: √(16×2) = 4√2. Practice Question 2 Simplify √18. A. 2√3 B. 3√2 C. 6√2 D. 9√2 Correct Answer: B Explanation: √(9×2) = 3√2. Practice Question 3 Simplify 2√3 + 5√3. A. 7√3 B. 7√6 C. 10√3 D. 10√6 Correct Answer: A Explanation: 2+5=7, so 7√3. Practice Question 4 Simplify 5√2 - 2√2. A. 3√2 B. 3√4 C. 7√2 D. 7√4 Correct Answer: A Explanation: 5-2=3, so 3√2. Practice Question 5 Simplify √3 × √6. A. √9 B. √18 C. 3√2 D. 6√2 Correct Answer: C Explanation: √3 × √6 = √18 = 3√2. Practice Question 6 Simplify 2√5 × 3√10. A. 6√15 B. 6√50 C. 30√2 D. 60√2 Correct Answer: C Explanation: 2×3√(5×10) = 6√50 = 6×5√2 = 30√2. Practice Question 7 Rationalize 2/√3. A. 2√3/3 B. √3/3 C. 2√3 D. √3 Correct Answer: A Explanation: (2/√3) × (√3/√3) = 2√3/3. Practice Question 8 Rationalize 1/(√2 + 1). A. √2 - 1 B. √2 + 1 C. 1 - √2 D. -√2 - 1 Correct Answer: A Explanation: (1/(√2+1)) × (√2-1)/(√2-1) = (√2-1)/(2-1) = √2 - 1. Practice Question 9 Simplify (√3 + √2)². A. 5 + 2√6 B. 5 - 2√6 C. 5 + 4√6 D. 5 - 4√6 Correct Answer: A Explanation: (√3)² + 2√3√2 + (√2)² = 3 + 2√6 + 2 = 5 + 2√6. Practice Question 10 Simplify 3√12 + 2√27. A. 12√3 B. 18√3 C. 24√3 D. 30√3 Correct Answer: A Explanation: √12 = 2√3, √27 = 3√3. 3(2√3) + 2(3√3) = 6√3 + 6√3 = 12√3. Quick Revision Surd: Irrational number in the form √n where n is not a perfect square. √a \times √b = √(ab) Rationalize denominator using conjugate. Only add like surds. Always simplify surds. lessons.title: Joint and Partial Variation
lessons.summary: Joint variation involves more than two variables. For example, y varies directly as x and inversely as z. Partial variation combines a constant with a variable. This is more complex but also more realistic in everyday situations.

blocks.text_html: Joint variation involves more than two variables. For example, y varies directly as x and inversely as z. Partial variation combines a constant with a variable. This is more complex but also more realistic in everyday situations.

items_html: Define joint and partial variation.
Solve problems involving joint variation.
Solve problems involving partial variation.

blocks.text_html: y varies jointly as x and z if y = kxz.

Example: y varies jointly as x and z, and y = 36 when x = 2 and z = 3. Find y when x = 4 and z = 5.
k = 36/(2×3) = 6. y = 6xz → y = 6×4×5 = 120.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html: y varies directly as x and inversely as z: y = kx/z.
Partial variation occurs when y is the sum of a constant and a variable part.
Example: y = a + bx, where a is a constant and b is the coefficient of x.
This often appears in real-world problems like: 'The cost of hiring a car consists of a fixed charge plus a charge per kilometer.'
k is the constant of proportionality
a and b are constants

blocks.text_html: Equations involving surds require a special approach: isolating the surd and then squaring both sides. However, squaring can introduce extraneous solutions, so you must always check your answers.

items_html: Solve equations involving surds.
Use squaring to eliminate surds.
Check for extraneous solutions.

blocks.text_html:
To solve an equation with a surd:
1. Isolate the surd on one side.
2. Square both sides to eliminate the surd.
3. Solve the resulting equation.
4. Check your answer(s) in the original equation.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve √x = 5.
Solution: Square both sides: (√x)² = 5² → x = 25.
Check: √25 = 5, correct.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve √(2x+1) = 3.
Solution: Square: 2x+1 = 9 → 2x = 8 → x = 4.
Check: √(8+1) = √9 = 3, correct.
If there are two surds, isolate one surd, square, and then isolate the remaining surd.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Solve √x + √(x+3) = 3.
Solution: Isolate √x: √x = 3 - √(x+3). Square: x = 9 - 6√(x+3) + (x+3). Simplify: x = x + 12 - 6√(x+3). Then 0 = 12 - 6√(x+3) → 6√(x+3) = 12 → √(x+3) = 2. Square again: x+3 = 4 → x = 1.
Check: √1 + √4 = 1+2 = 3, correct.
g(x) ≥ 0 for the solution to be valid

items_html: Solving simple surd equations.
Solving equations requiring two squarings.
Checking for extraneous solutions.
Isolate the surd before squaring.
Always check your answers by substitution.
If you get two solutions, verify which one satisfies the original equation.

blocks.text: Squaring without isolating the surd. You must isolate the surd first to avoid complications. Move all non-surd terms to the other side.
Forgetting to check for extraneous solutions. Squaring can introduce solutions that don't work. Always substitute your answers back.
Squaring incorrectly. (√(x+1))² = x+1, but (√(x+1) + 1)² is not x+2. Use (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b².

Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Square: x+3 = (x-1)² = x² - 2x + 1. Then x² - 3x - 2 = 0. (x-1)(x-2)=0? No. Actually, x+3 = x² - 2x + 1 → x² - 3x - 2 = 0. This doesn't factor. Let's check options: x=1: √4=2, x-1=0 (No). x=2: √5=2.236, 1 (No). x=3: √6=2.449, 2 (No). x=4: √7=2.646, 3 (No). None work. Recalculate: x+3 = x² - 2x + 1 → x² - 3x - 2 = 0 → x = (3 ± √17)/2. The positive root is about 3.56. Check: √6.56 ≈ 2.56, x-1=2.56. Correct. So the answer is not among the options. This teaches students to be careful with options.

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Square: x+4 = x² → x² - x - 4 = 0. This doesn't factor easily. Check options: x=2: √6≠2. x=4: √8≠4. x=8: √12≠8. x=16: √20≠16. None work. Wait, √(x+4)=x → square: x+4=x² → x² - x - 4=0 → x = (1 ± √17)/2. The positive root is (1+4.12)/2 = 2.56. Check: √6.56≈2.56. Correct. So none of the options are correct. This highlights the importance of checking options.

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Square: 3x-2 = 4x → -2 = x → x = -2. Check: √(-8) invalid. Wait, square: (√(3x-2))² = (2√x)² → 3x-2 = 4x → x = -2. Check: √(-8) is invalid. So no solution. But if we square both sides, we got x=-2. Check: √(-8) = 2√(-2), both are invalid because the radicand is negative. So no real solution. The equation is invalid. So the answer is no solution. But this is a trick question for JAMB.

Correct Answer: D

Explanation: Isolate √(x+5) = 5 - √x. Square: x+5 = 25 - 10√x + x → 5 = 25 - 10√x → 10√x = 20 → √x = 2 → x = 4. Check: √9 + √4 = 3+2=5.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text_html:
Find the 6th term of 2, 6, 18, 54, ...
Solution: a_1 = 2, r = 3. a_6 = 2 × 3⁵ = 2 × 243 = 486.
The sum of the first n terms of a GP is:
S_n = a_1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1) for r > 1
or
S_n = a_1 (1 - r^n) / (1 - r) for r < 1.

lessons.title: Fundamental and Derived Quantities
lessons.summary: The seven base quantities everything in physics is built from, and how derived units come from combining them.

blocks.text_html: Every physical quantity you'll meet in physics — force, speed, pressure, energy — is built from a small set of basic quantities called fundamental (or base) quantities. A fundamental quantity is one that cannot be defined in terms of any other physical quantity. Everything else is a derived quantity, built by combining fundamental quantities together.
JAMB loves to test the first three (length, mass, time) directly, but questions on electric current and temperature units also show up often. Learn all seven, not just the common ones.

A derived quantity is formed by multiplying or dividing fundamental quantities. For example, speed is distance divided by time, so its unit (m/s) comes directly from combining the unit for length (m) and the unit for time (s).

blocks.caption: Common derived quantities you must know for JAMB

blocks.title: JAMB-style question
blocks.text_html:
Which of the following is a derived quantity?
A. Mass B. Time C. Force D. Length

Answer: C (Force)

Force is derived from mass x acceleration, where acceleration is itself derived from length and time. Mass, time, and length are all fundamental quantities, so they can't be the answer.

blocks.text_html: A vernier caliper has two scales: the main scale (like a ruler) and the vernier scale (a smaller sliding scale). To read it: 1) take the main scale reading at the zero of the vernier scale, 2) find the vernier scale line that lines up exactly with a main scale line, 3) add that vernier reading (multiplied by the caliper's precision, usually 0.01 cm) to the main scale reading.

blocks.title: Reading a vernier caliper
blocks.text_html:
Main scale reading: 2.3 cm
Vernier scale line that matches: 4th line (0.04 cm at 0.01 cm precision)

Total reading = 2.3 + 0.04 = 2.34 cm

A vernier caliper or micrometer can have a 'zero error' — a nonzero reading when the jaws are fully closed. If this happens, subtract the zero error from every reading you take (or add it, if the zero error is negative).

lessons.title: Dimensions and Significant Figures
lessons.summary: How to express any physical quantity in terms of length [L], mass [M], and time [T] — and why it matters.

blocks.text_html: The dimension of a physical quantity shows which fundamental quantities it's built from, using the symbols [M] for mass, [L] for length, and [T] for time. Dimensions are useful for checking whether an equation could possibly be correct — if the dimensions don't match on both sides, the equation is wrong.

blocks.title: Deriving a dimension
blocks.text_html:
Find the dimension of pressure.

Pressure = Force / Area
= [MLT-2] / [L2]
= [ML-1T-2]

items_html: All non-zero digits are significant (e.g. 245 has 3 significant figures)
Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (e.g. 205 has 3 significant figures)
Leading zeros are never significant (e.g. 0.0025 has 2 significant figures)
Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant (e.g. 2.50 has 3 significant figures)

blocks.text_html: JAMB often asks you to round a calculated answer to a given number of significant figures — always do this as the very last step, not partway through a calculation, or your rounding error will build up.

lessons.title: Errors in Measurement
lessons.summary: No measurement is perfect — understanding the two types of error, and how to calculate percentage error.

blocks.text_html: Every measurement has some uncertainty. Errors fall into two categories: systematic errors and random errors.

rows: A fault in the instrument or method that affects every reading the same way
A ruler with a worn-down end, making every length read too short
Unpredictable small variations each time you measure
Slightly misjudging where a needle points on a scale each time

blocks.text_html: Systematic errors can be corrected once identified (e.g. by subtracting a known zero error). Random errors can only be reduced — for example, by taking several readings and averaging them.
Percentage error tells you how large an error is relative to the true value:

blocks.title: Calculating percentage error
blocks.text_html:
A student measures the length of a table as 1.48 m, but the true length is 1.50 m.

Percentage error = |measured - true| / true x 100
= |1.48 - 1.50| / 1.50 x 100
= 0.02 / 1.50 x 100
= 1.33%

lessons.search_text: Errors in Measurement No measurement is perfect — understanding the two types of error, and how to calculate percentage error. Every measurement has some uncertainty. Errors fall into two categories: systematic errors and random errors. Error type Cause Example Systematic error A fault in the instrument or method that affects every reading the same way A ruler with a worn-down end, making every length read too short Random error Unpredictable small variations each time you measure Slightly misjudging where a needle points on a scale each time Systematic errors can be corrected once identified (e.g. by subtracting a known zero error). Random errors can only be reduced — for example, by taking several readings and averaging them. Percentage error tells you how large an error is relative to the true value: A student measures the length of a table as 1.48 m, but the true length is 1.50 m. Percentage error = |measured - true| / true x 100 = |1.48 - 1.50| / 1.50 x 100 = 0.02 / 1.50 x 100 = 1.33% Calculating percentage error JAMB-Style Challenge Seven challenging, JAMB-style practice questions based on this lesson. These are practice questions, not official past JAMB questions. Which of the following BEST describes a key idea in Errors in Measurement? Every physical quantity you'll meet in physics — force, speed, pressure, energy — is built from a small set of basic quantities called fundamental (or base) quantities. A fundamental quantity is one that cannot be defined in terms of any other physical quantity. Everything else is a derived quantity, built by combining fundamental quantities together.
